snippet.title: How you are runing your portfolio
snippet.description:
How often do you check your portfolio?

Every time you open that app, you create an opportunity to react. And reacting — even with good intentions — is almost always the wrong move.

You see a fund down 8%. You feel something. You read about it. You look at alternatives. Forty minutes later you have either switched the fund, added a new one, or spent the next three days second-guessing everything.

That cycle does not make you a better investor. It makes you a busier one.

Busy and better are not the same thing.

What the best investors actually do:

Build a portfolio around a clear goal and timeline

Trust the structure they put in place

Review once a year — one question, one hour

Ask only this: am I still on track?

If yes — close the app

A portfolio built around a 7-year goal does not need monthly intervention. It needs time. Every interruption has a cost. The portfolio does its best work when you leave it alone.

snippet.title: The Shocking End of India’s Most Loved Bike Yamaha RX100
snippet.description:
The Shocking End of India’s Most Loved Bike Yamaha RX100
When Yamaha RX100 launched in 1985, it instantly became India’s dream bike.
Lightweight body, low price, and a powerful two-stroke engine that could hit 60 km/h in just 7 seconds — people started calling it the “Pocket Rocket.”

But this same speed slowly turned into its biggest problem.

Criminals began using RX100 for chain snatching and robberies, giving the bike a bad public image. On top of that, riders had to mix 2T oil with petrol, which caused heavy pollution.

Then came the final blow.

In 1996, the Indian government introduced strict emission norms, and RX100’s two-stroke engine failed to meet them. Yamaha had no option but to stop production completely.

This is the real story of how India’s most popular bike disappeared — not because people stopped loving it, but because the world around it changed.

snippet.title: Coca-Cola Invented Today’s Santa🎅🥤#shorts #youtubeshorts
snippet.description:
In the early 1900s, Coca-Cola helped redefine Santa Claus—and in doing so, boosted its declining winter sales. At the time, Coca-Cola struggled during colder months because people were less inclined to drink chilled beverages. To change this, the company launched a groundbreaking holiday marketing campaign featuring Santa Claus.

Coca-Cola portrayed Santa as a warm, cheerful, and friendly figure dressed in a red suit with a white beard—an image that aligned perfectly with the brand’s red-and-white identity. These illustrations, created for Coca-Cola’s Christmas advertisements in newspapers and magazines, were published consistently for decades. Over time, this version of Santa became deeply ingrained in popular culture and helped standardize the modern image of Santa Claus worldwide.

While Santa existed long before Coca-Cola, the brand played a major role in popularizing the iconic look we recognize today. This short explores how one of the smartest marketing strategies in history shaped a global Christmas symbol.

snippet.title: The 100-Year-Old Desi Drink
snippet.description:
This hakeem made a medicinal syrup 120 years ago to save people’s lives, and today most Indians and Pakistanis can’t live without it.

In 1907, Abdul Majeed, a hakeem of traditional Unani medicine, saw something horrifying - People were suffering from heatstrokes in Delhi’s burning summers.

Many people died as well.

But instead of prescribing medicines, he did something different.

Using his Unani expertise, he started mixing natural ingredients like rose petals and herbs to make a special syrup.

He called it Rooh Afza, meaning soul refresher, and he gave it to his patients to prevent heatstrokes.

What happened next was mind-blowing.

People started drinking it not as a medicine but as a refreshing summer drink. By the 1940s, it became a part of every Indian household. 

But then came 1947.

After partition, one of Majeed’s sons stayed in India, while the other moved to Pakistan and restarted the business from scratch.

But here’s the fascinating part.

Even after partition, Rooh Afza’s formula and popularity remained untouched. It remained equally popular on both sides of the border, used in water, milk, chuski, and falooda.

Today, Rooh Afza does 500 crores in annual sales, but it still uses the same formula from 1907 in the same nostalgic bottle.
